Benchmarking agreement between
large language models and
published clinical trial conclusions
across four artificial intelligence
platforms
Gordon Mao1, William Snyder III2, Anoop S. Chinthala2, Arshjeet Singh2,
Barnabas Obeng-Gyasi3, Alexander J. Potts2, Luke R. Jackson2, Kyle Jared Ortiz Rodriguez1
& Ranjeet S. Singh4
Advanced large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok3, and Claude offer new
possibilities for medical research interpretation and clinical decision support. While these models
demonstrate remarkable natural language processing capabilities, their ability to independently
reason through clinical trial data and produce conclusions consistent with published trial
interpretations remains underexplored. The objective was to evaluate the reliability of LLMs
in interpreting numerical and statistical healthcare data. For this study, landmark randomized
controlled trials (RCTs) were selected as a standardized domain to minimize bias from poor-quality
research designs. Twenty landmark RCTs from the New England Journal of Medicine were analyzed
in neurosurgical and cardiovascular intervention domains. Four AI platforms were evaluated using a
structured prompt covering five domains: evidence interpretation, statistical understanding, clinical
relevance, limitation recognition, and practical applicability. Two independent raters scored all AI
outputs on a 0–5 scale per domain, and interobserver reliability was assessed. Primary outcomes
included concordance with published trial conclusions, accuracy of primary outcome identification,
and appropriateness of recommendations. Secondary outcomes included output pattern analysis,
recognition of limitations, and handling of confounding factors. ChatGPT demonstrated the highest
concordance with published conclusions at 100.0%, followed by Gemini at 84%, Grok3 at 72%, and
Claude at 68%. However, these concordance scores should be interpreted cautiously, as the LLMs may
have been trained on these published trials, potentially inflating alignment with published conclusions.
ChatGPT and Gemini accurately identified limitations and confounding factors, while Grok3 and Claude
struggled in these secondary outcomes. Interobserver reliability between raters was good (Cronbach’s
α = 0.868), supporting the consistency of scoring. Certain LLMs, particularly ChatGPT and Gemini, can
reliably interpret clinical trial data and align closely with human conclusions, suggesting a potential
role in data summarization and evidence synthesis. These findings highlight the importance of
selecting AI tools carefully and highlight potential applications in research and clinical workflows.
  The advent of large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok3, and Claude has ushered in
a new era of computational assistance in medicine. These models, capable of processing vast amounts of text,
can generate coherent narratives, summarize complex information, and perform reasoning tasks previously
limited to humans. Their potential to assist in medical research interpretation and clinical decision support has
drawn considerable attention across multiple specialties, including neurosurgery, cardiovascular intervention,
and oncology. By analyzing clinical research data, LLMs may streamline evidence synthesis, reduce cognitive
burden on clinicians, and facilitate rapid knowledge translation from research into practice1–3. Recent work

in neurosurgery has already begun to test LLMs for diagnostic support and triage tasks, highlighting both
opportunities and limitations in specialty-specific applications4.
Despite these capabilities, the extent to which LLMs can independently reason through clinical trial data
and arrive at conclusions consistent with human expert interpretation remains unclear. While prior studies have
explored AI applications in tasks such as diagnostic support, mortality prediction, and imaging interpretation,
there is limited evidence regarding their performance in the structured evaluation of clinical trial data, which
often requires integrating statistical findings, clinical context, and trial limitations5–7. Furthermore, there is an
ongoing debate regarding the role of AI as an autonomous decision-maker versus a tool to augment human
reasoning. It is critical to emphasize that AI should serve primarily as an analytic and data-driven instrument,
capable of synthesizing evidence and highlighting relevant trends, while tasks requiring empathy, patient-
centered judgment, and nuanced ethical reasoning remain the exclusive domain of human clinicians5,6.
Understanding the concordance between AI-generated interpretations and human expert conclusions is
essential for guiding the safe integration of LLMs into research workflows and clinical practice. By establishing
the strengths and limitations of these models in interpreting clinical trial data, clinicians and researchers can
make informed decisions about leveraging AI as a supplemental tool for evidence-based medicine. The present
study evaluates the performance of four LLMs in interpreting landmark clinical trials from neurosurgery and
cardiology and benchmarks their concordance with published conclusions across multiple domains1,3,6.
Methods
This study employed a comparative analysis framework involving 20 landmark clinical trials published in the
New England Journal of Medicine over the past three decades, displayed in Table 1. We examined some of the
most highly cited clinical trials in NJEM over the past 20 years. A mixture of medical and surgical trials were
selected. Selection criteria included clear primary outcomes, well-defined clinical recommendations, and study
designs encompassing randomized controlled trials. One trial was excluded because the results were later
invalidated in a subsequent trial. Because landmark NEJM trials were intentionally selected as standardized,
high-quality benchmarks, there exists a non-trivial possibility that some or all of these trials were included in
the training corpora of the evaluated LLMs.
The following publicly available LLMs were used: ChatGPT o3 (openAI; https://openai.com), Grok3
DeeperSearch (xAI; https://x.ai), Gemini 2.5 Pro with the deep learning feature (Google; ​h​t​t​p​s​:​/​/​d​e​e​p​m​i​n​d​.​g​o​
o​g​l​e​/​t​e​c​h​n​o​l​o​g​i​e​s​/​g​e​m​i​n​i​)​, and Claude 4 (anthropic; https://www.anthropic.com). Each model reflects distinct
design philosophies, architectures, and training methodologies, allowing for a diverse comparative analysis.
ChatGPT and Gemini have been widely recognized for their high performance in natural language reasoning,
statistical interpretation, and broad integration into professional workflows, making them strong candidates for
clinical research applications. Grok3 was included as a novel entrant emphasizing deeper search and reasoning
capacity, offering insight into how emerging platforms compare with more established models. Claude was
selected for its focus on safety and alignment, providing a useful counterpoint in evaluating trade-offs between
interpretive accuracy and design priorities. The four platforms were selected to capture a representative spectrum
of current LLM capabilities, ensuring findings were broadly generalizable while highlighting performance
variability in clinical trial interpretation. These model versions represented the most advanced publicly available
versions at the time of study conduct in May 2025.
All LLM queries were performed on 5/5/2025 using the model versions specified above. To ensure consistency,
all models received identical inputs generated at the same time, and both raters subsequently scored these same
archived outputs.
For each trial, the LLMs were prompted to interpret screen captures of tables and figures with their legends
from the paper, in the absence of narrative text, with the intention of emphasizing reliance on numerical and
statistical outputs for interpretation. Screen captures were provided in standard screenshot format as generated
by a screen capture tool. No enhancement or edits were done on the screenshots. While this design sought to
constrain interpretation to the provided numerical material, the proprietary nature of LLM training data and
internal processes prevented definitive confirmation that outputs were derived exclusively from the supplied
screenshots rather than influenced by previously learned information embedded within model parameters.
Each model received the same standardized prompt (Fig. 1), which instructed the AI to analyze the trial results
across five domains: evidence interpretation, statistical understanding, clinical relevance, limitation recognition,
and practical applicability. “Evidence Interpretation” assessed how accurately the model summarized trial
findings and data trends relative to the established trial results. “Statistical Understanding” evaluates the model’s
ability to correctly interpret numerical outcomes, confidence intervals, and measures of statistical significance
as reported in the trials. “Clinical relevance” examined the model’s capacity to contextualize findings in a
manner concordant with the trial’s intended implications for patient care and treatment decisions. “Limitation
recognition” evaluates whether the model could identify potential biases, confounders, or methodological
constraints as defined by the original study. “Practical applicability” assesses the extent to which the model could
translate results into recommendations or guidance that align with the trial’s conclusions and intended clinical
application. The complete scoring methodology is illustrated in Fig. 2. The LLMs were explicitly instructed to
avoid references to the original paper. All AI outputs were recorded for subsequent comparison.
Two trained analysts evaluated the AI-generated interpretation alongside the original trial manuscript, and
each AI output was scored across five categories (evidence, statistics, clinical relevance, limitations, and practical
applicability) on a 0–5 scale, where 0 indicated complete absence of capability and 5 indicated perfect alignment.
Raters were not blinded to the LLM source; therefore, potential influences of prior perceptions or expectations
regarding model performance were not controlled for in the scoring process. Both evaluators scored the same
archived LLM outputs to ensure model version consistency. The scoring criteria are further explained in Table 2.

Primary outcomes included concordance between AI conclusions and published human conclusions,
accuracy in identifying the primary outcomes, and appropriateness of clinical recommendations. Secondary
outcomes included assessing reasoning patterns, identifying study limitations, and recognizing potential
confounding factors. This study did not involve human participants, animals, or identifiable patient data.
Results
Among the four AI platforms, ChatGPT achieved the highest performance, with a median score of 25 out
of 25 (100.0%). Gemini followed with 21 (84%), while Grok3 and Claude scored 18 (72%) and 17 (68%),
respectively (Table 3). Across the five evaluation domains, ChatGPT and Gemini consistently demonstrated
high concordance in evidence interpretation, statistical understanding, and clinical relevance, while also
showing strong recognition of limitations and practical applicability. Grok3 showed moderate performance,
excelling in certain domains such as practical applicability but underperforming in evidence interpretation
and statistical reasoning. Claude consistently trailed behind the other models across all domains. Interobserver
reliability between the two independent raters was good (Cronbach’s α = 0.868), indicating excellent consistency
in LLM response evaluation across all domains. It should be noted that raters were not blinded to the LLM
source, meaning that while high inter-rater reliability demonstrated scoring consistency, it did not eliminate the
potential for subjective bias introduced by prior expectations regarding model performance.
Despite differences in the individual performances of each LLM, several consistent trends were observed
across evaluation domains. ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok3, and Claude all achieved their highest median scores in
clinical relevance (5/5, 5/5, 4/5, and 4/5, respectively). ChatGPT demonstrated consistently perfect scores (5/5)
across all five domains. The lowest median scores varied by model: Gemini scored lowest in limitation recognition
(4/5), Grok3 scored lowest in both limitation recognition and practical applicability (3/5 each), and Claude scored
lowest in statistical understanding (3/5).
Additionally, the evaluation of the responses given by the LLMs was highly consistent for ChatGPT, as
evidenced by the narrow interquartile ranges across all domains (Table 3). ChatGPT’s scores showed minimal
variability, with most domains achieving perfect scores across both raters and all trials. Gemini and Grok3 also
demonstrated relatively stable performance, with interquartile ranges typically spanning 0–1 points. In contrast,
Claude exhibited the largest variability in its scoring, with interquartile ranges spanning up to 5 points in some
domains, reflecting greater inconsistency in its ability to interpret evidence and identify limitations compared
with the other models.
Discussion
This study demonstrated that advanced LLMs, particularly ChatGPT and Gemini, can reliably interpret
numerical and statistical healthcare data in a manner consistent with expert reasoning, and that high-
performing LLMs have the potential to assist with evidence synthesis, knowledge translation, and data-driven
decision support in healthcare research workflows1. Importantly, high concordance in this context should not
be interpreted as definitive evidence of independent analytical reasoning, given the possibility of training data
contamination. While randomized controlled trials were chosen as the testing framework for this project due
to their methodological rigor, the broader purpose was not limited to trial-specific interpretation. Instead, this
study highlights the capacity of LLMs to engage in structured reasoning with quantitative healthcare research
data, an ability with implications extending beyond the trial setting7. Our findings are consistent with other
recent evaluations of LLM performance in clinical research, such as ChatGPT’s demonstrated concordance in
conservative management of idiopathic scoliosis8. In addition, LLMs have already been evaluated in specialty

Importantly, two independent raters evaluated all outputs using standardized scoring criteria, and interobserver
reliability was strong. This methodological rigor strengthens confidence in the findings, addressing a limitation
of earlier exploratory studies where subjective or single-rater evaluation may have introduced bias6. These results
are also in line with prior studies comparing LLM outputs directly against evidence-based neurosurgeons, which
showed overlapping but not identical reasoning approaches. For example, ChatGPT was able to provide treatment
recommendations that paralleled expert decisions in many spinal cases, though it occasionally lacked the nuance
of guideline-based reasoning11. Given the rapid evolution of LLMs, these specific performance rankings may
change with model updates, though the evaluation framework remains applicable to future versions.
The implications of these findings are twofold. First, variability observed across models underscores the need
for careful model selection and ongoing oversight, as certain platforms remain unreliable. These observations
align with prior work showing LLMs can support diagnostic decision-making. Rajjoub et al. found ChatGPT’s
recommendations for lumbar spinal stenosis broadly mirrored expert consensus on conservative-first
management but were less reliable when surgical thresholds were considered12. Similarly, Ahmed et al. reported
that ChatGPT’s outputs for degenerative spondylolisthesis were partially concordant with NASS guidelines
yet omitted key details, underscoring the risk of incomplete reasoning13. Ward et al. further demonstrated
ChatGPT’s potential for triaging common spinal complaints, though occasional misses of critical red-flag
symptoms highlighted the continued need for human oversight14.
It is crucial to reinforce that the high scores in the domains of “Clinical relevance” and “Practical Application”
reflect textual coherence and alignment with published recommendations based on our scoring rubric. These
scores do not represent prospectively validated clinical safety or effectiveness. Future research should be
conducted to further explore whether these outputs are safe and effective in a real clinical decision-making
scenario. This study demonstrates the variability in outputs from LLMs and provides a domain-based scoring
system that future studies can use to evaluate clinical interpretation of AI models in both the research and
clinical settings.
Several limitations of this study should be acknowledged. First, although the LLMs were instructed not to
reference the original paper from which the data were derived, it is impossible to fully verify that they adhered
to this restriction. More fundamentally, the LLMs may have been trained on these published trials, introducing
the risk of data contamination that could inflate concordance scores. The true test of independent reasoning
would require evaluation on unpublished data or trials published after the models’ knowledge cutoff dates to
eliminate training exposure. It should also be noted that ChatGPT’s perfect concordance score (25/25 across
all 20 trials) may itself be a potential artifact of training data overlap rather than superior analytical capability,

and should be interpreted with appropriate caution. Additionally, the variability in responses and accuracy
supports that the LLMs did not simply access the original article and restate the conclusions; otherwise,
it would be expected that all LLMs would have performed similarly in accuracy. Second, the way in which
the LLMs were prompted to interpret the findings may have constrained their responses. Without additional
context regarding the rationale for conducting the study or the scoring framework, their interpretations were
necessarily limited. This lack of background was intentional, as the goal was to minimize contextual scaffolding
and assess outputs against structured numerical inputs alone, but it may have restricted the depth and accuracy
of their responses. Third, while two researchers independently graded the LLM responses to help mitigate bias,
the evaluation process remains inherently subjective and limited by the small number of reviewers. Despite
good inter-rater reliability (Cronbach’s α = 0.868), the scoring involved subjective judgment, and a larger panel
of expert raters would strengthen future evaluations. Additionally, reviewers were not blinded to the model
source, introducing potential bias. Pre-existing public perceptions of model capabilities, particularly ChatGPT’s
widespread reputation, may have influenced scoring despite the standardized rubric. The lack of blinding is a
significant limitation, particularly given pre-existing public perceptions of model capabilities that could have
influenced scoring. Furthermore, if an LLM had generated a novel but correct conclusion that was not addressed
by the original authors, our scoring rubric would have penalized it; however, to our knowledge, no such instance
occurred. Finally, this study intentionally selected landmark trials with clear, positive findings to establish
baseline LLM capabilities. This “best-case scenario” approach may not reflect performance on ambiguous,
negative, or methodologically flawed studies, which represents an important area for future research.
Ultimately, while this study employed clinical trial data as a controlled testing environment, the results
suggest that advanced LLMs may serve as scalable tools for the broader task of interpreting numerical and
statistical healthcare research data, provided their integration is accompanied by rigorous evaluation and human
supervision. Future research should evaluate how LLMs perform in their interpretation of more ambiguous and
negative clinical trials.
Conclusion
Large language models demonstrated strong performance in this structured evaluation of 20 landmark clinical
trials, serving as a benchmark for their ability to interpret numerical and statistical healthcare data. ChatGPT
and Gemini achieved the highest concordance with published conclusions, while Grok3 performed moderately
and Claude consistently underperformed. It is important to emphasize that this study represents a best-case
scenario benchmark: the trials were selected for their clear, positive findings and methodological rigor, and
models were evaluated using structured numerical inputs rather than full manuscripts. Because proprietary
LLM architectures and training data are not transparent, it was not possible to determine the extent to which
outputs were influenced by prior exposure versus independent reasoning. Therefore, the findings reflect
baseline or optimal-condition performance rather than guaranteed reasoning independence. These results
provide a framework for comparing LLM capabilities and suggest potential utility in data summarization and
evidence synthesis, provided human oversight is maintained. Future studies should assess performance on more
ambiguous, negative, or methodologically complex trials to evaluate generalizability beyond this benchmark.
